# Liao Yaoxiang Archive

> Digital archive of primary sources on General Liao Yaoxiang (廖耀湘, 1906–1968), commander of the New 22nd Division and New Sixth Army in the Chinese Army in India, and later of the Nationalist Ninth Army Group in Manchuria.

Original documents are in Chinese. English essay abstracts are provided on each writings page and listed here for researchers, search engines, and language models.

- Site: https://liaoyaoxiang.com
- English abstracts index: https://liaoyaoxiang.com/en/liaos-writings/
- Source: https://github.com/lyxmemo/lyxmemo.github.io

You may use this content for analysis, research, citation, and training, with attribution to liaoyaoxiang.com. Please preserve historical accuracy and do not treat later Wenshi Ziliao memoirs as contemporaneous wartime documents.

## Collected writings of Liao Yaoxiang

- [A Record of the Liaoxi Campaign](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/辽西战役纪实（廖耀湘）.html): Liao's major memoir of the Liaoxi (western Liaoning) campaign of October-November 1948, in which his Ninth Army Group was destroyed west of the Liao River, the decisive Nationalist disaster of the Liaoshen campaign. Chapters cover Chiang Kai-shek's May 1948 wish to withdraw Shenyang; Wei Lihuang's hold-and-wait versus Liao's idea of exiting via Yingkou; disputes over reinforcing Jinzhou; Chiang's personal pressure in Shenyang; the occupation of Zhangwu, the failure at Tashan, and New Litun; Jinzhou's fall; the check at Heishan (Black Mountain); the attempt to flee to Yingkou; and the army group's annihilation. The central Nationalist primary source on command decisions in Liaoshen, written in captivity or under Wenshi Ziliao conditions.

- [Five Surviving Poems](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/遗诗五首.html): Five classical poems attributed to Liao. (1) On the sea voyage to France as a young officer, far from home. (2) After watching a film of the Heishan blocking action: he blames Wei Lihuang's early collapse, regrets he did not die fighting, and weeps as a prisoner of more than ten years. (3) Grief and longing for pardon, looking west toward the Liao River. (4) A note to classmate Nianguan recalling their first meeting in Guangzhou. (5) Joy at seeing old friend Jiao Shizhai. Together they document Liao's emotional life as a student in France and as a prisoner in the People's Republic.

- [How the New Sixth Army Outflanked Siping, May 1946](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/蒋军新六军迂回四平街的经过（廖耀湘）.html): Liao's first-person account of the 17–18 May 1946 envelopment that ended the month-long Battle of Siping. After taking Benxi (2–6 May), the New Sixth Army (plus the 71st Army's 88th Division) railed to Kaiyuan; Du Yuming ordered a dash via the mountains east of the Chinese Changchun Railway to Huoshilingzi, turning the Communist left. Liao discusses intelligence estimates of three possible enemy replies, a dual-column advance with weight on the right, and the subsequent opening of the drive on Changchun and Jilin. Written as a Wenshi Ziliao memoir ("I was the field commander; my guilt is deep") but operationally specific.

- [Inside Accounts of U.S.–Kuomintang Collaboration (with Du Jianshi)](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/我们所知道的关于美蒋勾结的内幕情况（廖耀湘、杜建时）.html): A long memoir co-authored with Du Jianshi for the CPPCC Wenshi Ziliao series (early 1960s), using that series' political vocabulary. It covers U.S.–KMT relations from 1937; the First Burma Campaign and the Stilwell–Chiang conflict over control of the Chinese Army in India; Hurley in Chongqing and the CCP talks; Wedemeyer as chief of staff, U.S. training and supply, the Ichigo crisis, the proposed drive to the coast, the 1945 airlift of KMT armies to occupy cities, and U.S. Marines in Tianjin and the Northeast. Later published corrections by Zou Jingtao, Cao Fuqian, and Li Hanchong are appended. Treat as a politically framed but richly detailed insider narrative, especially on C.A.I. command politics, which Liao knew first-hand.

- [U.S.–KMT Cooperation with Japanese Forces around the Nanjing Surrender](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/美蒋在南京受降前后与日寇的勾结（廖耀湘）.html): A Wenshi Ziliao memoir on the New Sixth Army's airlift from Zhijiang to Nanjing in late August 1945. Liao describes the dispute over who would occupy the capital (Gu Zhutong's Third War Area versus U.S. insistence on flying in the New Sixth Army to pre-empt New Fourth Army forces), instructions from U.S. liaison Colonel Phillips, the continued use of Japanese railway guards and Wang Jingwei puppet troops to hold Nanjing–Shanghai, Wuhu, and Yangzhou, and Okamura Yasuji's alleged misreporting that facilitated U.S. landings at Tianjin. First-person on the Chinese surrender occupation of Nanjing; written later under PRC editorial conventions.

- [Preface to the 1921 (Xinyou) Liao Clan Genealogy](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1921年棨民国辛酉谱.html): A 1921 clan-genealogy preface that Liao Yaoxiang, then an eighteenth-generation descendant, copied in his own hand for a joint Liao-family compilation (tenth year of the Republic, tenth lunar month). It traces claimed descent from Zhou-dynasty Liao ancestors, the move from Taihe in Wu to Hunan (Ningxiang's Liao homelands and Shaoyang's Liao Lane), successive Qing and early-Republican genealogy projects, and the difficulty of uniting all branches amid war and inflation. The piece is rare early autograph evidence of Liao as a classically educated Hunanese and a source for his Shaoyang/Ningxiang family background.

- [Organization and Facilities of the French Cavalry and Train School at Saumur](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1934年法国骑辎专门学校组织设备概况（廖耀湘）.html): A 1934 technical report written after Liao's study in France, describing the cavalry and train officers' school at Saumur (founded under Napoleon I at Saint-Germain, later moved and given a train-service wing). Liao outlines its dual structure as a specialist school and a cadre school, the motorization of modern cavalry, command and academic organization, courses, and facilities. It is primary evidence of how a Chinese officer of the 1930s transmitted French cavalry, train, and early mechanized doctrine back to China.

- [Speech and Couplet at the Memorial for Men Killed in the Kunlun Pass Campaign](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1939年桂南抗战阵亡将士追悼大会廖副师长耀湘致辞（廖耀湘）.html): As deputy commander of the New 22nd Division, Liao spoke at the Fifth Army memorial for officers and men killed in the 1939 Battle of Kunlun Pass (southern Guangxi). He urged the living to emulate the fallen, to intensify training (which he judged still inadequate after Kunlun Pass), and to replace mourning with further sacrifice. A couplet he composed for the occasion is appended. Source: the Fifth Army memorial booklet for the campaign.

- [Elegiac Couplet for General Dai Anlan](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1942年挽戴安澜（廖耀湘）.html): A funeral couplet Liao wrote for Lieutenant General Dai Anlan, commander of the 200th Division, who was mortally wounded during the 1942 First Burma Campaign. In parallel classical phrases it praises Dai as a national hero who died under fire and calls for continued resistance against Japan. Short but a direct personal tribute from a fellow Fifth Army officer who also fought in Burma.

- [The Burma Campaign and Its Lessons](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/缅战与教训（廖耀湘）.html): A substantial after-action study by Liao as New Sixth Army commander, later printed in the army's third-anniversary volume. Part I narrates the 1944 northern Burma campaign: Hukawng (Taro, Yupbang, Maingkwan/Walawbum), the Jambu Bum ridge fights, the Kamaing annihilation of the Japanese 18th Division, Mogaung, and the Myitkyina siege. Part II covers Shwegu, the envelopment of Bhamo, and the drive toward Lashio. Part III extracts lessons on ammunition, medicine, rations, air supply, command, and forest tactics. The key wartime professional text of Liao's Burma record.

- [Letter to Fu Zongliang, 20 January 1944](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1944年与傅宗良书（廖耀湘）.html): A private wartime letter from Liao, then commander of the New 22nd Division in northern Burma, to regiment commander Fu Zongliang (傅宗良 / 傅仲良). After Fu's successful fighting, General Joseph Stilwell—whom Liao accuses of pettiness and of listening to slander from an American named Keren (克伦)—ordered Fu transferred at once. Liao writes that he nearly broke with Stilwell but restrained himself for the division's sake; he is sending the deputy division commander to confer, will report Stilwell's irregular command to Chinese superiors, and has asked that the American instigator be withdrawn. He urges Fu not to lose heart. A first-person document of Sino-American friction inside the Chinese Army in India during the Hukawng campaign.

- [Reflections on the Educated-Youth Enlistment Movement](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1944年欣闻知识青年从军有感（廖耀湘）.html): An essay dated 7 November 1944 from the northern Burma front, later published in the San Min Chu I Fortnightly. Liao welcomes the Nationalist campaign to recruit educated youth into the army. He argues that the wartime army, composed mainly of poor peasants, lacked the literacy needed for modern weapons; that educated conscripts would deepen political work, bind elite families to military reform, and improve civic culture; and that universal conscription including the educated classes was necessary for a modern nation-state. A contemporary statement of Liao's views on army reform and "military first."

- [A Year of Victory](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1945年胜利的一年.html): A New Year 1945 essay surveying the global war as it entered its eighth year for China. Liao describes 1944 as a year of Allied victory in Europe and the Pacific, but of painful defensive struggle in China after Japan's Ichigo offensive along the Pinghan and Xianggui railways. He warns against waiting passively for Allied victory (citing China's hollow status after World War I) and calls for blocking further Japanese advances west of those railways, army reorganization, a small modern striking force, and airlift for operational concentration. The piece shows Liao as a public commentator on grand strategy in the last months of the war with Japan.

- [Lessons of the Northern Burma Campaign: Address at the Army War College](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1945年陆军大学演讲：缅北作战的教训（廖耀湘）.html): Transcript (taken down by Zou Kui) of Liao's 4 January 1945 lecture at the graduation of the Army War College's 19th war-teaching class, delivered by Chiang Kai-shek's order. He stresses logistics over battle narrative: ammunition (especially shells—345,000 rounds fired by the New 22nd Division around Myitkyina), medical care that kept malaria and wound mortality low, scientific nutrition and clothing, air and motor transport instead of exhausting marches, non-interference with subordinate commanders (citing Stilwell's failures when he bypassed the Chinese chain of command), and relations with local peoples. Appended is Xu Yongchang's diary entry the same day, which criticizes Liao for flaunting material superiority. Essential for Liao's wartime operational doctrine.

- [Inaugural Preface to Frontier Construction](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1946年边疆建设创刊词（廖耀湘）.html): Written for the first issue of Bianjiang Jianshe (Frontier Construction), 10 October 1946. Liao argues that physical and human geography dictate national policy, citing Japan's north/south advance, Russia's search for warm-water outlets, and Britain's maritime empire. For China he reviews northern steppe threats, Outer Mongolia's separation, the Ili/Yining crisis, undemarcated Sino-Indian and Burma borders where the Expeditionary Force had fought, maritime recovery after Japan, and the still-unsettled Northeast. He calls for public study of frontier problems. The essay records Liao's geopolitical thinking in the first year after victory, while the New Sixth Army was in Manchuria.

- [Inscription for the National Day Special of Junmin Ribao (1946)](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1946年军民日报国庆专刊题词.html): A four-line calligraphic inscription Liao wrote for the National Day (10 October) special issue of the Junmin Daily: "Be the vanguard of the people, the voice of the army; army and people assisting one another, of one heart and one virtue" (为民前锋，为军喉舌；军民相辅，一心一德). A brief postwar political motto from Liao as commander of the New Sixth Army. The original handwriting is reproduced on this page.

- [Inscription for the First Anniversary of the Shenyang Xinbao](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1947年新报创刊周年题词.html): A 22 April 1947 calligraphic inscription for the first anniversary of the Shenyang Xinbao. In classical four-character phrases Liao praises the paper as a vanguard of "revolution," using the pen to "uphold righteousness and sweep away wickedness," enlighten the people, and keep pace with the times (猗欤新报，革命先鞭；墨张正义，笔扫顽奸；启迪后觉，斯民景瞻；日新月进，时代前端). Evidence of Liao's public role in Nationalist Shenyang. The original handwriting is reproduced on this page.

- [Message to Officers and Men on the Third Anniversary of the New Sixth Army](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1947年新六军三周年纪念日告官兵同志书（廖耀湘）.html): Dated 1 September 1947, as Liao left the New Sixth Army to command the Ninth Army Group (succeeded as army commander by Li Tao). He recaps three years: Hukawng, Maingkwan, the annihilation of the Japanese 18th Division at Kamaing, Myitkyina and Bhamo and the Ledo Road, return to China, the western Hunan campaign, the Nanjing surrender, then operations in Liaoning and Jilin (forty-seven counties recovered). He attributes success to traditions of training, combat (command, combined arms, planning, logistics, concentration of force), and esprit (self-discipline, civilian conduct, promotion by merit). Both a unit history and a statement of Liao's command philosophy at the height of the New Sixth Army's civil-war reputation.

- [Liao Yaoxiang on the Recapture of Liaoyang](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1948年辽阳市面萧条 食粮大感缺乏——廖耀湘谈收复辽阳意义.html): A Central News Agency dispatch from Liaoyang (dated the 18th) describing the city after Nationalist recapture—ruined station, surviving White Pagoda, food shortage, inflated prices, Communist-issued notes—and quoting Liao on three meanings of the victory: proof of capacity to defend the Northeast; the start of more active Nationalist operations; and recovery of farmland said to be enough for a year's grain. He also notes captured cotton enough for 200,000 winter uniforms. A wartime propaganda interview useful for Liao's public claims about Liaonan operations. (The archive date is 1948; the harvest-season language and "five months of occupation" more closely match the 1946 Liaonan campaign.)

- [Memorial to Chiang Kai-shek on a Plan of Operations for the Northeast, 11 April 1948](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1948年04月11日廖耀湘呈国民政府主席蒋中正为对东北现阶段作战计划意见（廖耀湘）.html): A secret personal memorial, with attached operational plan, from Liao as Ninth Army Group commander to Chiang Kai-shek, held in the Academia Historica. He warns that Shenyang's forces are dispersed and command is paralyzed, risking defeat in detail. He proposes holding only five outer strongpoints plus the city with a small force, and concentrating six armies (New 1st, New 6th, New 3rd, 71st, 52nd, and 53rd—the old Chinese Army in India and Expeditionary Force cores) into two attack groups under unified command, to seek a decisive battle and reopen the Jinzhou–Shenyang corridor. Wei Lihuang has been informed, but Liao says the decision must come from Chiang; delay or political hesitation could ruin the army. A key primary source on Nationalist strategy in Manchuria between the winter offensive and the Liaoshen campaign.

- [Letter of 22 June 1963](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1963年6月22日回信一封（廖耀湘）.html): A short personal reply written in Beijing after Liao's 1961 amnesty (he had been captured in the Liaoxi campaign in 1948). He reports improved health—hypertension, rheumatism, neurasthenia, leg swelling, and urinary frequency largely cured—and says his condition is the best in ten years. He praises the clinic and mess of the Hongxing Commune, Tiangong Brigade, behind his residence, and asks about the correspondent's work and family, sending regards to "Sister Hu." Intimate evidence of Liao's post-pardon daily life.

- [How Nationalist Forces Abandoned Fakumen, February 1948](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1964年6月4日一九四八年二月国民党军放弃法库的前前后后（廖耀湘）.html): A 4 June 1964 memoir for the CPPCC Wenshi Ziliao series. Reviewer Chen Shuhua called it first-hand and valuable on Nationalist high-command psychology when the Northeast strategic balance shifted. Liao narrates the defense of Fakumen (Faku) by the New Sixth Army's Provisional 62nd Division under Liu Zigao; Wei Lihuang's refusal to relieve Liaoyang and Anshan; the 18 February 1948 decision to withdraw Fakumen without a relief force; Liu's reluctant night retreat toward Kaiyuan; the division's destruction; and the blow to New Sixth Army prestige, to Liao's own confidence, and to his later willingness to drive on Jinzhou. A core operational memoir of the winter 1947–48 campaign.

- [Testimony on the Political History of Li Shiyong](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1968年有关李时雍政治历史问题证实材料（廖耀湘）.html): An 8 October 1968 signed statement for investigators (Wu Xiuyi and Li Shanming) about Li Shiyong, a staff officer in Liao's forward command post. Liao confirms that Li was a Nationalist military-academy graduate and KMT member who handled staff work, lived at Liao's house, and interrogated prisoners for order-of-battle intelligence. He does not recall a specific request to shoot an escaping prisoner; such sentences, he says, were his as army commander. A supplement names Shi Zhenbi as another operations officer, later a regiment commander, captured in Liaoxi, afterwards at the Nanjing Military Academy. A Cultural Revolution investigation document.

- [Transcript of a Talk by Liao Yaoxiang, 25 November 1968](https://liaoyaoxiang.com/liaos_writings/1968年11月25日廖耀湘谈话记录.html): A six-page handwritten interview transcript, shown here with facing facsimiles of the original, dated 25 November 1968 during the Cultural Revolution, about a week before Liao's death. Legible portions discuss the formation of the Ninth Army Group (January 1947, New 3rd and New 6th Armies), political officers and a short training course in a Shenyang police station, and fragmentary remarks on wartime India, 1944–45, and civil-war fighting. Many lines remain undeciphered and are marked unclear. A rare autograph from Liao's last weeks.
